{{short description|Two-colour symmetry (examples, history and dimensional counts)}}
[[File:Dichromatic triangle.jpg|thumb|Dichromatic triangle illustrating colour symmetry]]
'''Dichromatic symmetry'''<ref name="Loeb">Loeb, A.L. (1971). ''[[Color and Symmetry]]'', Wiley, New York, {{ISBN|9780471543350}}</ref>{{snd}}also called '''antisymmetry''',<ref name=Shubnikov1951>Shubnikov, A.V. (1951). ''Symmetry and antisymmetry of finite figures'', Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR, Moscow</ref><ref  name="Colored Symmetry" /> '''black-and-white symmetry''',<ref>Gévay, G. (2000). ''Black-and-white symmetry, magnetic symmetry, self-duality and antiprismatic symmetry: the common mathematical background'', Forma, 15, 57–60</ref> '''magnetic symmetry''',<ref>Tavger, B.A. (1958). ''The symmetry of ferromagnetics and antiferromagnetics'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., '''3''', 341-343</ref> '''counterchange symmetry''',<ref>Woods, H.J. (1935). ''The geometric basis of pattern design part I: point and line symmetry in simple figures and borders'', Journal of the Textile Institute, Transactions, '''26''', T197-T210</ref> or '''dichroic symmetry'''<ref>Makovicky, E. (2016). ''Symmetry through the eyes of old masters'', de Gruyter, Berlin, {{ISBN|9783110417050}}</ref>{{snd}}is a [[symmetry operation]] which reverses an object to its opposite.<ref>Atoji, A. (1965). ''Graphical representations of magnetic space groups'', American Journal of Physics, '''33'''(3), 212–219, {{doi|10.1119/1.1971375}}</ref> A more precise definition is "operations of antisymmetry transform objects possessing two possible values of a given property from one value to the other."<ref name="Mackay">Mackay, A.L. (1957). ''[https://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0365110X57001966 Extensions of space-group theory]'', Acta Crystallogr. '''10''', 543-548, {{doi|10.1107/S0365110X57001966}}</ref> Dichromatic symmetry refers specifically to two-coloured symmetry; this can be extended to three or more colours in which case it is termed [[polychromatic symmetry]].<ref>Lockwood, E.H. and Macmillan, R.H. (1978). ''[[Geometric symmetry (book)|Geometric symmetry]]'' [https://books.google.com/books?id=OvQ8AAAAIAAJ&dq=polychromatic+symmetry+lockwood&pg=PA67 {{nbsp}}], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 67-70 & 206-208 {{ISBN|9780521216852}}</ref> A general term for dichromatic and polychromatic symmetry is simply colour symmetry. Dichromatic symmetry is used to describe [[Magnetic space group|magnetic crystals]] and in other areas of physics,<ref name=Padmanabhan>Padmanabhan, H., Munro, J.M., Dabo, I and Gopalan, V. (2020). ''Antisymmetry: fundamentals and applications'', Annual Review of Materials Research, '''50''', 255-281, {{doi|10.1146/annurev-matsci-100219-101404}}</ref> such as [[T-symmetry|time reversal]],<ref>Shubnikov, A.V. (1960). ''Time reversal as an operation of antisymmetry'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., '''5''', 309-314</ref> which require two-valued symmetry operations.

== Examples ==

A simple example is to take a white object, such as a triangle, and apply a colour change resulting in a black triangle. Applying the colour change once more yields the original white triangle.
[[File:Antiidentity operation.svg|thumb|center|upright=1.5|Anti-identity operation and [[Cayley table]]]]

The colour change, here termed an anti-identity operation (1'), yields the identity operation (1) if performed twice.

Another example is to construct an anti-mirror reflection (m') from a [[Reflection symmetry|mirror reflection]] (m) and an anti-identity operation (1') executed in either order.

[[File:Anti-reflection animation.gif|thumb|center|upright=1.5]]

The m' operation can then be used to construct the antisymmetry [[point group]] 3m' of a dichromatic triangle.

[[File:Dichromatic D3 (3m' point group) operations.svg|thumb|center|upright=1.5|The six operations making up the dichromatic D3 (3m') point group]][[File:D3 Cayley table with colour change.svg|thumb|right|D3 Cayley table with colour change representing the antisymmetry group 3m']]

There are no mirror reflection (m) operations for the dichromatic triangle, as there would be if all the smaller component triangles were coloured white. However, by introducing the anti-mirror reflection (m') operation the full [[Dihedral group of order 6|dihedral D3]] symmetry is restored. The six operations making up the dichromatic D3 (3m') point group are:
* identity ({{math|e}})
* rotation by {{math|2''&pi;''/3}} ({{math|r}})
* rotation by {{math|4''&pi;''/3}} ({{math|r{{sup|2}}}})
* anti-mirror reflection ({{math|m'}})
* combination of {{math|m'}} with {{math|r}} ({{math|m'r}})
* combination of {{math|m'}} with {{math|r{{sup|2}}}} ({{math|m'r{{sup|2}}}}).

Note that the vertex numbers do not form part of the triangle being operated on - they are shown to keep track of where the vertices end up after each operation.

== History ==

In 1930 [[Heinrich Heesch]] was the first person to formally postulate an antisymmetry operation in the context of examining the 3D [[space group]]s in 4D.<ref name=Heesch>Heesch, H. (1930). ''Über die vierdimensionalen Gruppen des dreidimensionalen Raumes'', Z. Krist., '''73''', 325-345, {{doi|10.1524/zkri.1930.73.1.325}}</ref> Heesch's work was influenced by Weber's 1929 paper on black-and-white colouring of 2D bands.<ref name=Weber>Weber, L. (1929). ''Die Symmetrie homogener ebener Punktsysteme'', Z. Krist., '''70''', 309-327, {{doi|10.1524/zkri.1929.70.1.309}}</ref>

In 1935–1936 H.J. Woods published a series of four papers with the title ''The geometrical basis of pattern design''. The last of these<ref>Woods, H.J. (1936). ''The geometric basis of pattern design part IV: counterchange symmetry in plane patterns'', Journal of the Textile Institute, Transactions, '''27''', T305-320</ref> was devoted to counterchange symmetry and in which was derived for the first time the 46 dichromatic 2D point groups.

The work of Heesch and Woods were not influential at the time, and the subject of dichromatic symmetry did not start to become important until the publication of [[Alexei Vasilievich Shubnikov|A.V. Shubnikov]]'s book ''Symmetry and antisymmetry of finite figures'' in 1951. Thereafter the subject developed rapidly, initially in Russia but subsequently in many other countries, because of its importance in [[magnetic structure]]s and other physical fields.

* 1951 [[Lev Landau|Landau]] and [[Evgeny Lifshitz|Lifshitz]] reinterpret black and white colours to correspond to time reversal symmetry<ref>Landau, L.D. and Lifshitz E.M. (1951). ''Course of theoretical physics, vol. 5. Statistical physics'', 1st edition, Nauka, Moscow</ref>
* 1952 W. Cochran re-derives the 46 dichromatic 2D point groups quoting the previous work of Alexander and Herrmann (1928–9) and Woods 1935<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cochran |first1=W. |title=The symmetry of real periodic two-dimensional functions |journal=Acta Crystallographica |date=10 September 1952 |volume=5 |issue=5 |pages=630–633 |doi=10.1107/s0365110x5200174x}}</ref>
* 1953 [[Alexander Mihailovich Zamorzaev|Zamorzaev]] derives the 1651 3D antisymmetric space groups for the first time<ref name=Zamorzaev>Zamorzaev, A.M. (1953). '' Generalization of the space groups'', Dissertation, Leningrad University</ref><ref>Zamorzaev, A.M. (1957). ''[https://archive.org/details/crystallography-reports_january-february-1957_2_1/page/10/mode/2up  Generalization of Fedorov groups]'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., 2, 10-15</ref>
* 1956 [[Ben Zion Tavger|Tavger]] and Zaitsev use the concept of vector reversal of [[magnetic moment]]s to derive point groups for magnetic crystals<ref>Tavger, B.A. and Zaitsev, V.M. (1956). ''Magnetic symmetry of crystals'', Soviet Physics JETP, '''3'''(3), 430-436</ref>
* 1957 [[Nikolay Belov (geochemist)|Belov]] and his colleagues independently derive the 2D and 3D antisymmetric groups<ref name=Belov>Belov, N.V., Neronova, N.N. and Smirnova, T.S. (1957). ''[https://archive.org/details/crystallography-reports_may-june-1957_2_3/page/310/mode/2up Shubnikov groups]'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., '''2'''(3), 311-322</ref>
* 1957 Zamorzaev and Sokolov begin the generalization of antisymmetry by introducing the concept of more than one kind of two-valued antisymmetry operation<ref  name=Padmanabhan /><ref>Zamorzaev, A.M. and Sokolov, E.I. (1957). ''[https://archive.org/details/crystallography-reports_january-february-1957_2_1/page/4/mode/2up Symmetry and various kinds of antisymmetry of finite bodies]'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., '''2'''(1), 5-9</ref><ref>Zamorzaev, A.M. and Palistrant, A.F. (1980). ''Antisymmetry, its generalizations and geometrical applications'', Z. Krist., '''151''', 231-248, {{doi|10.1524/zkri.1980.151.3-4.231}}</ref><ref>Zamorzaev, A.M. (1988). ''[https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82277227.pdf Generalized antisymmetry]'', Comput. Math. Applic., '''16'''(5-8), 555-562, {{doi|10.1016/0898-1221(88)90245-3}}</ref>
* 1957 [[Alan Lindsay Mackay|Mackay]] publishes the first review of the Russian work in English.<ref name="Mackay" /> Subsequent reviews were published by Holser (1961),<ref>Holser, W.T. (1961). ''[https://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0365110X61003612  Classification of symmetry groups]'', Acta Crystallogr., '''14''', 1236-1242, {{doi|10.1107/S0365110X61003612}}</ref> [[Vladimir Alexandrovich Koptsik|Koptsik]] (1968),<ref>Koptsik, V.A. (1968). ''A general sketch of the development of the theory of symmetry and its applications in physical crystallography over the last 50 years'', Sov. Phys. Cryst., '''12'''(5), 667-683</ref> [[Rolph Ludwig Edward Schwarzenberger|Schwarzenberger]] (1984),<ref>Schwarzenberger, R.L.E. (1984). ''Colour symmetry'', Bull. London Math. Soc., '''16''', 209-240, {{doi|10.1112/blms/16.3.209}}</ref> in [[Branko Grünbaum|Grünbaum]] and [[Geoffrey Colin Shephard|Shephard]]'s ''[[Tilings and patterns]]'' (1987),<ref>Grünbaum, B. and Shephard, G.V. (1987). ''[[Tilings and patterns]]'', W.H. Freeman, New York, {{ISBN|9780716711933}}</ref> and Brückler and Stilinović (2024)<ref>Brückler, F.M. and Stilinović, V. (2024) ''From friezes to quasicrystals:  a history of symmetry groups'', 1823-1864, {{doi|10.1007/978-3-030-19071-2_132-2}}, in Sriraman, B. (ed.) ''Handbook of the history and philosophy of mathematical practice'', Springer, pp 3200, {{ISBN|978-3-030-19071-2}}</ref>
* Late 1950s [[M.C. Escher]]'s artworks based on dichromatic and polychromatic patterns popularise colour symmetry amongst scientists<ref>MacGillavry, C.H. (1976). ''[[Symmetry aspects of M. C. Escher's periodic drawings]]'', International Union of Crystallography, Utrecht, {{ISBN|9789031301843}}</ref><ref>Schnattschneider, D. (2004). ''[[M. C. Escher: Visions of Symmetry]]'', Harry. N. Abrams, New York, {{ISBN|9780810943087}}</ref>
* 1961 Clear definition by [[Bartel Leendert van der Waerden|van der Waerden]] and [[Johann Jakob Burckhardt|Burckhardt]] of colour symmetry in terms of [[group theory]], regardless of the number of colours or dimensions involved<ref>van der Waerden, B.L. and Burkhardt, J.J. (1961). ''Farbgruppen'', Z. Krist, '''115''', 231-234, {{doi|10.1524/zkri.1961.115.3-4.231}}</ref>
* 1964 First publication of Shubnikov and Belov's ''[[Colored Symmetry (book)|Colored Symmetry]]'' in English translation<ref name="Colored Symmetry">Shubnikov, A.V., Belov, N.V. et al. (1964). ''Colored symmetry'', ed. W.T. Holser, Pergamon, New York</ref>
* 1965 [[Wladyslaw Opechowski]] and Rosalia Guccione provide a complete derivation and enumeration of the dichromatic 3D space groups<ref>Opechowski, W. and Guccione, R. (1965). ''Magnetic symmetry'' in ''Magnetism, vol. IIA'' ed. Rado, G.T. and Suhl, H., Academic Press, New York, pp 105-165</ref>
* 1966 Publication by Koptsik of the complete atlas of dichromatic 3D space groups<ref>Koptsik, V.A. (1966). ''Shubnikov groups: Handbook on the symmetry and physical properties of crystal structures'', Moscow University, Moscow</ref> (in Russian)
* 1971 Derivation by [[Arthur Lee Loeb|Loeb]] of 2D colour symmetry configurations using rotocenters<ref name="Loeb" />
* 1974 Publication of ''[[Symmetry in Science and Art]]'' by Shubnikov and Koptsik with extensive coverage of dichromatic symmetry in 1D, 2D and 3D<ref name=Shubnikov>Shubnikov, A.V. and Koptsik, V.A. (1974). ''Symmetry in science and art'', Plenum Press, New York, {{ISBN|9780306307591}} (original in Russian published by Nauka, Moscow, 1972.)</ref>
* 1988 Washburn and Crowe apply colour symmetry analysis to cultural patterns and objects<ref>Washburn, D.K. and Crowe, D.W. (1988). ''[[Symmetries of Culture: Theory and Practice of Plane Pattern Analysis]]'', Washington University Press, Seattle, {{ISBN|9780295970844}}</ref>
* 2008 [[John Horton Conway|Conway]], Burgiel and [[Chaim Goodman-Strauss|Goodman-Strauss]] publish ''[[The Symmetries of Things]]'' which describes the colour-preserving symmetries of coloured objects using a new notation based on [[Orbifold]]s<ref>Conway, J.H., Burgeil, H. and Goodman-Strauss, C. (2008). '' The symmetries of things'', A.K. Peters, Wellesley, MA, {{ISBN|9781568812205}}</ref>
